metadata.title: SubViewports
metadata.audience: people making games in Godot, and anyone directing an AI that writes shaders for them
metadata.lecture_opening_description: Draw into a picture, then shade the picture
metadata.bookend_exempt_reason: lecture skill: opens on the narrated identity card then the hesitant writer; no composer cold open.

beats.narration_text: Sub Viewports. Learn how a Sub Viewport draws part of your game into a picture, and how to shade that picture with a second shader.

beats.narration_text: Hallo. This is Liam, in for Bear. Most people think shaders cannot see each other's work: one shader, one node, and no way to build on what another drew. A Sub Viewport changes that. One shader can shade the picture another shader made.

props.text:

each other's work.

beats.motion_claim: The writer types the assumption a newcomer arrives with and corrects it into the film's real subject.

qc.sparse_reason: Hesitant-writer bookend: the correction is the motion.

beats.narration_text: Five terms. A shader is a small program the graphics card runs to decide how something is drawn. A texture is an image a shader can read. A viewport is a rectangle the engine draws into. U V is a point's address on a shape. And alpha is how visible a pixel is.

terms.meaning: a small program the graphics card runs to decide how something is drawn
an image a shader can read by address
a rectangle the engine draws into
a point's address on the shape: 0 to 1 across, 0 to 1 down
how visible a pixel is: 0 invisible, 1 solid

beats.act: I · A Picture Off to the Side
beats.narration_text: A sprite spins. Rainbow stripes slide across it, and a ripple runs through the whole picture. Two shaders made this, one after the other. The second shades what the first one drew. The trick is drawing into a picture, not onto the screen.

beats.act: I · A Picture Off to the Side
beats.narration_text: That picture comes from a Sub Viewport: a node that draws its children into a picture of its own, not onto the screen. Drawn, but not shown directly: that is what off-screen means. Sprites, text, interface, even a three-D scene can go inside.

A teal blob fades into the small square, then a text glyph 'Aa', a small button outline and a three-line cube join it. The screen stays empty the whole time. Caption under the square: 'off-screen: drawn, not shown directly'; a one-line definition on the square: 'draws its children into a picture of its own'.

beats.act: I · A Picture Off to the Side
beats.narration_text: On its own, a Sub Viewport shows nothing. Its picture is a Viewport Texture: a texture that keeps the latest drawing. Give that texture to a sprite, and the sprite shows the picture.

shot.visual_intent: Code card with the one real line at left; at right a real Godot window on the cream stage: empty for seven seconds, then the picture appears (a teal blob in a mid-grey box, the viewport's clear colour) at the moment the line runs.

cues.label: ViewportTexture: the viewport's latest picture

shot.motion_claim: The stage is empty until the texture is handed over, then the picture appears.

lecture.why: Nothing on screen, then the picture on the very line that makes it appear, is the claim as a cause and an effect.

beats.act: I · A Picture Off to the Side
beats.narration_text: In the editor, add a Sub Viewport node and give it a size. Put a sprite inside it. Add a second sprite outside. In the second sprite's Texture slot, open the menu, and under New choose Viewport Texture. Then pick the Sub Viewport.

beats.act: I · A Picture Off to the Side
beats.narration_text: In code, it is five lines. Make the viewport, give it a size, add it to the scene, put the sprite inside, and hand its texture to the display.

shot.visual_intent: Left: a code card with five real lines (monospace): var sub := SubViewport.new() / sub.size = Vector2i(512, 512) / add_child(sub) / sub.add_child(inner_sprite) / display.texture = sub.get_texture(). Right: a diagram that builds with the focused line: a small tree 'Main' on top, a dashed box, a screen frame at the lower right. Line 1 draws the dashed box ('sub'); line 2 writes '512 x 512' along its edges; line 3 hooks it under 'Main'; line 4 drops a teal blob into it; line 5 draws an arrow from the box to a display sprite on the screen, and the blob appears on the screen.

beats.act: I · A Picture Off to the Side
beats.narration_text: The size is the picture's resolution, in pixels. A new Sub Viewport is five hundred twelve pixels square. Shrink it to a hundred twenty-eight, draw it four times bigger, and the pixels show. Set the sprite's Filter to Nearest, and they turn into crisp blocks.

shot.visual_intent: Two real displays of the same blob, both 512 px across on the stage: left a 512 px picture drawn 1:1 (crisp), right a 128 px picture drawn 4x (soft with the Linear filter). Partway, the right display's Filter switches to Nearest and the soft edge turns into hard blocks.

show.event: 512 px and 128 px pictures side by side
Filter: Nearest; the edge turns into blocks

props.videoLabel: Godot 4.7.2 · Forward+ · scripted: Filter switches at 12.5 s
props.caption: resolution: how many pixels the picture holds

shot.motion_claim: The right picture is soft, then snaps into crisp blocks when the filter changes.

lecture.why: The softness and the blocks are the claim; only the real render shows what the engine does to a small picture.
lecture.capture_spec: C03 (scene c03): two opaque viewports, 512 and 128 px (blob drawn natively at each size), displays at x = 100 and x = 668, the right at scale 4; Filter Linear until 12.5 s (on the words "Filter to Nearest"), then Nearest. 19 s, Forward+. beats.act: I · A Picture Off to the Side
beats.narration_text: Inside the viewport, the top-left corner is the origin, and the picture covers only positive x and y from there. A centered sprite placed at zero, zero has three quarters of itself outside. The eyes are gone.

beats.act: I · A Picture Off to the Side
beats.narration_text: See the box around the sprite? That is the picture's background, filled with the project's clear color. Turn on Transparent B G, and the empty parts become see-through. Now whatever is behind the picture shows through.

shot.visual_intent: Code card with one line at left; at right the display over a faint grey grid: first the picture's mid-grey box hides the grid, then at the moment the line runs the box vanishes and the grid shows through, leaving only the blob.

show.event: Transparent BG on; the box vanishes

cues.label: Transparent BG: empty parts become see-through

props.videoLabel: Godot 4.7.2 · Forward+ · scripted: Transparent BG on at 8 s

shot.motion_claim: The box disappears and the grid behind it shows through.

lecture.why: A box that vanishes to reveal what was behind it is the claim; the grid makes the see-through visible.
lecture.capture_spec: C05 (scene c05): grid of 2 px lines every 64 px behind the display, opaque picture until 8.0 s then `transparent_bg = true`; 15 s, Forward+. Verified (run-7a): the empty pixel is the clear colour (0.659, 0.627, 0.565) before and the stage (0.851, 0.835, 0.792) after; the picture's empty pixel alpha goes from 1 to 0.

beats.act: I · A Picture Off to the Side
beats.narration_text: One catch with see-through pictures, which hard edges hide. A half-transparent pixel is stored already multiplied by its alpha. Draw it the usual way, and soft edges come out too dark. Set the Blend Mode to Premultiplied Alpha, and they come out right.

shot.visual_intent: One real display of a soft gold glow over the faint grid. It starts with Blend Mode Mix: a muddy dark ring surrounds the glow. At the moment the blend mode changes to Premultiplied Alpha the dark ring vanishes and the glow is clean. A terracotta ring marks the dark ring; readouts name the two blend modes.

show.event: Premultiplied Alpha: the ring is gone

props.videoLabel: Godot 4.7.2 · Forward+ · scripted: Blend Mode changes at 10.5 s
props.caption: premultiplied: each color already multiplied by its alpha

shot.motion_claim: The dark ring around the glow vanishes the moment the blend mode changes.

lecture.why: The ring that vanishes is the claim; arithmetic would explain it, but the real glow is what a viewer will meet.
lecture.capture_spec: C06 (scene c06): picture 512 transparent, glow image (gold, alpha falling to 0 over the outer 45 % of its radius) over the grid; the display uses a CanvasItemMaterial, Blend Mode Mix until 10.5 s then Premultiplied Alpha; 18 s, Forward+. Verified (run-7a, run-5 G1) at ring pixel (807, 360): Mix (0.655, 0.608, 0.490), Premultiplied (0.890, 0.800, 0.576), the glow drawn directly (0.890, 0.796, 0.576).

beats.narration_text: Now give each side a shader. The inner shader sits on the sprite inside the viewport. The outer shader sits on the sprite that shows the picture. The inner one draws first. The outer one gets the finished picture.

shot.visual_intent: Act title 'Two Shaders, One Result' (serif 40) top-left. Left: the SubViewport square with the teal blob inside and a small tag 'inner shader' on the blob. A wide arrow labelled 'picture' runs right to a display sprite on a screen frame carrying a tag 'outer shader'. A token (a few teal dots) starts on the blob, turns gold passing the inner tag, rides the arrow, and on reaching the display passes the outer tag and is re-tinted. Small words 'first' under the left half and 'then' under the right.

token rides the arrow as a picture

shot.motion_claim: A token passes the inner shader first, travels as a picture, then passes the outer shader.

beats.narration_text: In the editor, that is each sprite's Material slot. The inner sprite's Material holds a Shader Material with the inner shader. The display's Material holds one with the outer shader. Each shader sits on its own node.

shot.visual_intent: Three real frames of the whole Godot editor window, cross-dissolving: (1) subviewports_E4-1_inner-sprite-material: the inner Sprite2D selected, its Inspector's Material group open with the Material slot holding a ShaderMaterial, ring on Material; (2) subviewports_E4-2_display-material: the Display sprite selected, the same slot, ring on Material; (3) subviewports_E4-5_shader-editor: the shader editor open at the bottom showing the outer shader's text (04-stripes).

beats.narration_text: The inner shader is an ordinary one. Its fragment function runs once for each pixel and sets the color. This one blends the sprite from teal at the top to gold at the bottom, using U V, the sprite's own address.

beats.narration_text: The outer shader gets the picture as its texture. It starts with one line that sets Premultiplied Alpha, and one line that copies the picture through unchanged. The result matches the picture exactly. Everything the inner shader made is already in there.

beats.narration_text: Now change something only the outer shader can. Multiply the picture by U V x, and it fades from nothing at the left edge to full at the right. Multiply the whole color, not only the alpha, because the picture's colors already carry their alpha.

beats.narration_text: The gradient turns with the sprite. The fade stays put. A shader's U V belongs to the thing it draws. The inner shader draws the sprite, and the sprite turns. The outer shader draws the picture, and the picture does not.

beats.narration_text: That is also the limit. By the time the outer shader runs, the sprites are gone. Only their pixels remain, already flattened together. It cannot ask a sprite where it is, or reach what hides behind another.

beats.narration_text: Resolution splits the same way. The inner shader works in the picture's pixels. The outer shader works in the display's pixels. Here a small picture is drawn big under an outer shader that draws stripes: the picture is coarse, the stripes are sharp.

shot.visual_intent: A real display of a 64 px picture drawn eight times bigger with the Nearest filter: the blob is built from big square blocks, while moving stripes drawn by an outer shader slide across it with crisp one-pixel edges that cut through the blocks at any position. Readouts 'picture pixels' and 'display pixels'.

props.videoLabel: Godot 4.7.2 · Forward+ · scripted: nothing but the stripes move

shot.motion_claim: The stripes' edges slide smoothly through the blocks of the blob, never snapping to them.

lecture.why: Smooth edges cutting through coarse blocks is the claim; only a live render shows that the two shaders live at different resolutions.
lecture.capture_spec: C12 (scene c12): transparent viewport 64 px (blob 64 px wide), display at scale 8 (512 px) with Nearest filter and 05-stripes-moving; 18 s, Forward+. Verified (run-6 X4, run-7b): the blob's own edges fall on multiples of 8 display pixels (x = 104 and 408 in run-6); the stripe edges do not (mod 8 = 7, 2, 5, 7, 2, 5, 7 in run-6; other values in run-7b, since the stripes move with TIME). Numbers are at scale 1; the 3x route multiplies them by 3.

beats.narration_text: A fade is one kind of mask. Stripes are another. Start with a diagonal: add the two U V numbers together. The sum climbs from zero at the top left to two at the bottom right, and equal values line up along diagonals.

shot.visual_intent: Act title 'Stripes and Hue' (serif 40) top-left. A square picture (the kit's UV square: 0 to 1 axes, y pointing down) with thin grey isolines along its diagonals at u + v = 0.5, 1 and 1.5. A ramp strip along the diagonal reads 0 to 2 with end labels '0' and '2'. A terracotta dot travels from the top-left corner to the bottom-right corner with a live label 'u + v'.

show.event: dot leaves the top-left corner, sum climbing

beats.narration_text: Let's recap with Claude. A Sub Viewport draws its children into a picture, and a Viewport Texture shows it anywhere. An inner shader makes the picture, and an outer shader shades it, using the picture's own U V. Stripes are a saw wave cut by a step, and a hue function colors them. Cut a mesh into a grid, and the outer vertex function can bend the whole picture.
